pos: n. (Nathaniel William Taylor, 1786–1858, professor of didactic theology at Yale and author of the New Haven theology)
etymology: Hebrew Nethane'l, gift of God; English occupational surname Taylor, a cutter of cloth.
biblical_def: Nathaniel William Taylor was pastor of the First Church in New Haven and then the first Dwight Professor of Didactic Theology in the Yale divinity school, where he taught for thirty-six years. He set out to defend Calvinism against Unitarian attack by removing what he judged its indefensible parts, and the result was a system the Reformed churches could not own. He denied that Adam's guilt is imputed to his posterity, holding that sin consists only in sinning; he taught that depravity is a universal certainty but that every man retains power to the contrary, a native ability to choose otherwise at any moment; and he made regeneration the sinner's own act of changing his governing purpose, with the Spirit persuading rather than quickening. Rom 8:7 is the verse his system cannot hold: the carnal mind “is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ability as the power to perform, whether physical or moral, and depravity as corruption, a vitiated state of the heart.
webster_full: ABIL'ITY, n. Physical power, whether bodily or mental; natural or acquired; force of understanding; skill in arts or science.
DEPRAV'ITY, n. Corruption; a vitiated state; as the depravity of manners and morals. A vitiated state of the heart; wickedness; corruption of moral principles.
REGENERA'TION, n. In theology, new birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God and his law are subdued.
scriptures: Rom 8:7
Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
corruption_summary: He defended Calvinism by removing imputation and inability, and what remained was not Calvinism.
corruption_paragraphs: Taylor's formula was certainty with power to the contrary: every man will certainly sin, and every man is at every moment able not to. The phrase sounds careful and it empties the doctrine of depravity of content, because a corruption that leaves the faculty entire is not the corruption Scripture describes. Joh 6:44 is decisive: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44). Can is the word in dispute, and Christ uses it of inability, not of reluctance.

The dictionary names the system by its own name, the New Haven theology, and names its effect. Eph 2:1 describes the natural man as “dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1), and Jer 13:23 asks whether the Ethiopian can change his skin. Taylor's revision made regeneration a self-wrought change of purpose, which is semi-Pelagian in substance however Augustinian in vocabulary, and it supplied the theological warrant for the revival technique that followed. The Reformed answer is not that man lacks a will but that his will is in bondage, and that God gives a new heart, Eze 36:26, rather than persuading an old one.
roots_summary: Greek phronema (G5427), the mind, its bent; dunamai (G1410), to be able; nekros (G3498), dead.
roots_lines: Greek phronema (G5427) — the mind, its bent; Romans 8:7.
Greek dunamai (G1410) — to be able, to have power; John 6:44.
usage: “neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7) — the clause his system removes.
“No man can come to me” (Joh 6:44) — inability, stated by Christ.
“dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) — not merely reluctant.

pos: n. (the system taught at Yale by Nathaniel William Taylor and his successors, c. 1820–1860, revising original sin, inability and regeneration)
etymology: From New Haven, Connecticut, seat of Yale College; theology, from Greek theos and logos.
biblical_def: New Haven Theology is the name given to the doctrinal system that came out of the Yale divinity school under Nathaniel William Taylor and spread through New England Congregationalism and the New School Presbyterian party. Its distinguishing tenets were that sin consists only in voluntary acts and never in an inherited nature; that Adam's guilt is not imputed to his descendants; that every man possesses a natural power to obey God at any moment; that regeneration is the sinner's own change of ruling purpose under the Spirit's persuasion; and that the atonement is a general provision rendering salvation possible for all rather than securing it for the elect. Its practical fruit was the revival method of the 1820s and 1830s, in which an immediate decision is pressed as something fully within the hearer's power. Rom 3:11 is the standing refutation: “There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God” (Rom 3:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imputation as the act of charging to the account of another, and inability as want of power, or want of competent means.
webster_full: IMPUTA'TION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution; the reckoning to one of what belongs to another.
INABIL'ITY, n. Want of power; impotence; want of adequate means; incapacity.
ATONE'MENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury.
scriptures: Rom 3:11
There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God.
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
Joh 1:13
Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
corruption_summary: A system built to make Calvinism defensible, which surrendered the four doctrines that made it Calvinism.
corruption_paragraphs: The New Haven men were answering a real pressure. Unitarianism was advancing in eastern Massachusetts and accusing orthodoxy of making God the author of sin and of condemning men for a guilt not their own. Taylor's answer conceded the premise: he relocated sin entirely in the act, so that nothing is charged to a man that he did not personally do. The concession costs Rom 5:12 and Psa 51:5 together, and with them the parallel on which Paul builds justification, since the same reckoning that imputes Adam's sin imputes Christ's righteousness.

The dictionary names the system semi-Pelagian in substance. 1Co 2:14 states what the natural man cannot do: he “receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God” (1Co 2:14), and cannot know them. Joh 1:13 makes the new birth not of the will of man but of God, and Eze 36:26 describes the giving of a new heart rather than the persuasion of an old one. The system's legacy runs directly into the decisionism of modern evangelism, in which a technique administered to an unregenerate will is trusted to produce a birth only God can give.
roots_summary: Greek suniemi (G4920), to understand; psuchikos (G5591), natural, of the soul; Hebrew chadash (H2319), new.
roots_lines: Greek psuchikos (G5591) — natural, animal, of the soul; 1 Corinthians 2:14.
usage: “There is none that understandeth” (Rom 3:11) — against native ability.
“receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God” (1Co 2:14) — the natural man's incapacity.
“nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Joh 1:13) — whose act the new birth is.

pos: n. (the doctrine of the will taught by Nathaniel William Taylor: certainty of sinning with native power to the contrary)
etymology: From the surname Taylor + Greek -ismos, denoting a system or doctrine.
biblical_def: Taylorism is the shorthand by which nineteenth-century American divines named one specific doctrine within the New Haven theology: Nathaniel William Taylor's account of the human will. Taylor held that moral agency requires a native power to choose either way at the moment of choosing, that this power is never lost by the fall, and that depravity is therefore a certainty of sinning rather than an incapacity to do otherwise. The formula was stated as certainty with power to the contrary. Its consequences are not confined to anthropology: if the will is unimpaired, effectual calling becomes persuasion, election becomes God's foresight of who will use the power well, and grace becomes assistance rather than resurrection. Rom 9:16 forecloses the whole line, that it is “not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines will as the faculty of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action, and liberty as freedom from restraint.
webster_full: WILL, n. That faculty or power of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action; the faculty which is exercised in deciding, among two or more objects, which we shall embrace or pursue.
LIB'ERTY, n. Freedom from restraint, in a general sense, and applicable to the body, or to the will or mind.
BOND'AGE, n. Slavery or involuntary servitude; captivity; imprisonment; restraint of a person's liberty by compulsion.
scriptures: Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
Joh 1:13
Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
Eph 2:5
Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)
corruption_summary: A formula about the will that quietly rewrites election, calling, and grace.
corruption_paragraphs: The attraction of Taylorism is that it seems to rescue responsibility. If a man could not have done otherwise, how is he blameworthy? The Reformed answer, held by the dictionary, is that the inability is moral and not physical: the sinner is unable because he is unwilling at the root, and the bondage is his own, which is precisely why he is guilty. Rom 8:7 says the carnal mind cannot be subject to God's law, and the cannot is the measure of the corruption, not an excuse for it.

The downstream cost is the point. Tit 3:5 says God saved us “according to his mercy he saved us” (Tit 3:5), by the washing of regeneration; Eph 2:5 says He quickened us when we were dead. A doctrine of unimpaired power turns both into descriptions of divine encouragement. The dictionary therefore treats Taylorism not as an eccentric opinion about psychology but as the hinge on which a whole generation of American theology swung away from the confessions it still professed.
roots_lines: Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to wish; Romans 9:16.
Greek suzoopoieo (G4806) — to quicken together with; Ephesians 2:5.
usage: “not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth” (Rom 9:16) — the verse the formula must evade.
“by the washing of regeneration” (Tit 3:5) — an act done to the sinner.
“hath quickened us together with Christ” (Eph 2:5) — resurrection, not assistance.

pos: n. (Bennet Tyler, 1783–1858, Connecticut Congregationalist, president of the Theological Institute of Connecticut and chief opponent of the New Haven theology)
etymology: English surname Tyler, one who lays tiles; Bennet, from Latin benedictus, blessed.
biblical_def: Bennet Tyler pastored at South Britain and Portland, served briefly as president of Dartmouth, and in 1834 became the first president and professor of theology at the Theological Institute of Connecticut at East Windsor, founded expressly as an orthodox alternative to Yale. He is remembered for the Tyler–Taylor controversy, conducted in pamphlets over more than a decade, in which he pressed three questions Taylor could not answer within his own system: whether depravity is a state of the heart prior to any act, whether regeneration is God's act or the sinner's, and whether the Spirit's work in conversion differs in kind from moral persuasion. Tyler held Psa 51:5 and Rom 5:12 as teaching a nature corrupt from conception, and he held that a man born again is born of God. Jud 1:3 describes what he did with his life: he contended earnestly for the faith once delivered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines controversy as a dispute, particularly in writing, and orthodox as sound in the Christian faith.
webster_full: CON'TROVERSY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions. A dispute is commonly oral, and a controversy in writing.
OR'THODOX, a. Sound in the Christian faith; believing the genuine doctrines taught in the Scriptures.
SEM'INARY, n. A place of education, in which young persons are instructed in the several branches of learning.
scriptures: Psa 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
Gal 1:9
As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: He founded a seminary because the pamphlets had not been enough.
corruption_paragraphs: Tyler's controversy is a model of how doctrinal dispute ought to be conducted and of how little it accomplishes by itself. He answered Taylor in print, carefully and at length, and Taylor kept the chair and the students. So Tyler and his party built a rival institution, which is what men do when the argument is sound and the institution is lost. The question he kept returning to is the one that decides the system: is there a corruption of nature prior to any act? Psa 51:5 answers it, “I was shapen in iniquity” (Psa 51:5).

The dictionary stands with Tyler. Rom 5:12 teaches that death passed upon all men because all sinned in the one man, which is imputation, and the New Haven denial of it unravels justification at the other end. Gal 1:9 gives the seriousness: the apostle repeats his anathema on another gospel rather than letting it stand as a variant opinion. Tyler was accused of a quarrelsome spirit, as men in his position always are; the accusation is the ordinary tax on contending, and Jud 1:3 commands the contending anyway.
roots_summary: Hebrew chul (H2342), to be brought forth; Greek anathema (G331), accursed; epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly.
roots_lines: Hebrew chul (H2342) — to be brought forth, shapen; Psalm 51:5.
usage: “I was shapen in iniquity” (Psa 51:5) — corruption prior to act.
“so death passed upon all men” (Rom 5:12) — the imputation denied at New Haven.
“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jud 1:3) — what he did for a decade.

pos: n. (Edwards Amasa Park, 1808–1900, Andover professor, last systematizer of the New England theology)
etymology: English surname Park, from a dweller by an enclosed ground; named for Jonathan Edwards.
biblical_def: Edwards Amasa Park taught at Andover Theological Seminary for more than fifty years and was the last and ablest defender of the New England theology as a distinct tradition descending from Jonathan Edwards through Edwards the younger, Smalley, Emmons, and Taylor. His 1850 address, The Theology of the Intellect and That of the Feelings, distinguished the language of doctrine stated for the understanding from the language of piety addressed to the affections, and argued that much apparent disagreement between orthodox parties is a confusion of the two registers. Charles Hodge answered him at length in the Princeton Review, holding that the distinction, however useful pastorally, becomes a device for holding two inconsistent doctrines at once. Park also edited the collected works of Emmons and wrote the standard memoirs of the school. Isa 8:20 is the test Hodge applied and the dictionary applies with him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines intellect as the faculty of the human soul which receives and compares ideas, and feeling as the sense of touch, or an emotion of the mind.
webster_full: IN'TELLECT, n. That faculty of the human soul or mind, which receives or comprehends the ideas communicated to it by the senses or by perception, or other means.
FEEL'ING, n. The sense of touch; the sensation produced by the touch; also, an emotion or passion of the mind.
DOC'TRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principle or position in any science; whatever is laid down as true by an instructor or master.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: He distinguished the theology of the intellect from that of the feelings, and the distinction became a hiding place.
corruption_paragraphs: Park's distinction has a real use. Scripture does speak of God in the language of affection and of relenting, and a dogmatician who flattens every such passage into a proposition will misread the Psalms. But Hodge saw the danger and named it: once the two registers are separated in principle, a man may preach what he does not hold and hold what he does not preach, and the doctrinal statement ceases to govern the pulpit. Tit 1:9 requires the elder to hold fast the faithful word so that he may “exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — one word, serving both purposes.

The dictionary's judgment is that Park's scheme functioned as the last refuge of a tradition that had already surrendered imputation and inability and wished to keep the Edwardsean name. Eph 4:14 describes the result of such flexibility: men “carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14). Andover's subsequent history, in which the seminary moved to the progressive theology of the 1880s within a generation of Park's retirement, is the evidence. A distinction that cannot be cashed out in propositions will not hold a seminary.
roots_summary: Greek didache (G1322), teaching; anemos (G417), wind; elegcho (G1651), to convince, reprove.
roots_lines: Greek psuchikos (G5591) — natural, of the soul; 1 Corinthians 2:14.
usage: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the test Hodge applied.
“carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — where the distinction led.
“to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — one word for both registers.

pos: n. (Leonard Woods, 1774–1854, first professor of theology at Andover Theological Seminary)
etymology: English surname Woods, a dweller by the wood; Leonard, from Germanic, lion-strong.
biblical_def: Leonard Woods was the first Abbot Professor of Christian Theology at Andover and taught there for thirty-six years. He had been instrumental in the compromise between the moderate Calvinists and the Old Calvinists that made the seminary possible in 1808, and he drafted the Andover creed which every professor was required to subscribe every five years. His Letters to Unitarians answered Henry Ware and William Ellery Channing on the deity of Christ, the atonement, and human depravity, and his five-volume collected works set out a moderate Calvinism that held imputation, inability, and definite atonement while pressing the free offer of the gospel on all. He opposed the New Haven revisions and he opposed the drift of his own younger colleagues. Tit 1:9 names the duty he discharged for three decades: holding fast the faithful word as he had been taught.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a creed as a brief summary of the articles of Christian faith, and subscription as the act of signing one's name in attestation.
webster_full: CREED, n. A brief summary of the articles of Christian faith; a symbol; a formula of belief.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of subscribing or writing one's name underneath; attestation by writing the name.
UNITA'RIAN, n. One who denies the doctrine of the Trinity, and ascribes divinity to God the Father only.
scriptures: Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
corruption_summary: He wrote the creed his successors subscribed and then watched them reinterpret it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Andover creed is one of the clearest lessons in American church history about confessional subscription. It was tight, it was renewed every five years, and within forty years of Woods's death the faculty was teaching a progressive theology while still signing it, on the ground that the words admitted a broader construction. Heb 10:23 commands us to “hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23), and a profession held with mental reservation is not held.

Woods's controversy with the Unitarians shows the other side of the man. Against Channing he argued the deity of Christ and the real satisfaction of the atonement, and against the New Haven men he argued inability; the two defences come from one principle, that the words of Scripture bind. Gal 1:8 is why he refused to call the Unitarian scheme a variety of Christianity. 2Ti 1:9 grounds the salvation he preached in God's own purpose and grace given before the world began, which is the doctrine the Andover of 1890 no longer taught.
roots_summary: Greek antechomai (G472), to hold fast; homologia (G3671), profession, confession; prothesis (G4286), purpose.
roots_lines: Greek antechomai (G472) — to hold fast, cling to; Titus 1:9.
usage: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9) — thirty-six years of it.
“hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23) — what subscription means.
“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — why Unitarianism was not a variety.

pos: n. (Moses Stuart, 1780–1852, Andover professor of sacred literature, father of American biblical philology)
etymology: Hebrew Mosheh, drawn out; Scottish surname Stuart, a steward.
biblical_def: Moses Stuart taught sacred literature at Andover for thirty-eight years and did more than any other American of his generation to put Hebrew and Greek study on a scholarly footing in this country. He wrote the first serviceable American Hebrew grammar, set up a press that could print Hebrew and Arabic type, translated German grammatical and lexical works, and trained the men who became the first generation of American orientalists, Edward Robinson among them. He wrote commentaries on Hebrews, Romans, Revelation, and Daniel, and he answered Channing on the Trinity and the deity of Christ in a public exchange that established him nationally. He also introduced the tools of German criticism to American seminaries, and used them himself to argue for a shortened canon of the Old Testament apocryphal borderlands and for readings his own colleagues judged unsafe. 2Ti 2:15 is the standard his students inherited, “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines philology as the study of language and its etymology, and grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety.
webster_full: PHILOL'OGY, n. Primarily, a love of words, or a desire to know the origin and construction of language; criticism; grammatical learning.
GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.
CRIT'ICISM, n. The art of judging with propriety concerning any object; the examination of literary works.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: He gave America the tools of biblical scholarship, and the tools arrived with their German assumptions attached.
corruption_paragraphs: Stuart's achievement is real and the dictionary does not diminish it. A church that cannot read its own Scriptures in the original languages is at the mercy of whoever can, and Stuart ended that dependence for American Protestantism. His exchange with Channing is a model of exegetical polemic, and his insistence that a text means what its grammar and usage allow is the right instinct, the same instinct Isa 8:20 commands.

The corruption to name is the freight. Stuart imported Gesenius and the German grammarians, and with them came the governing premise of that scholarship, that the biblical books are to be read as the ordinary products of their period, with predictive prophecy and Mosaic authorship open to revision on internal grounds. Stuart himself resisted much of this, but his successors at Andover did not, and the documentary hypothesis and the division of Isaiah entered American seminaries through doors he had built. 2Pe 1:21 is the premise the dictionary holds against the whole method: the prophecy came not by the will of man, but “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21).
roots_summary: Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; phero (G5342), to bear, be moved; Hebrew torah (H8451), law.
roots_lines: Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, rightly divide; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek spoudazo (G4704) — to be diligent, study; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, carry, be moved; 2 Peter 1:21.
usage: “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — what he trained men to do.
“holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) — the premise the method lost.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — his own best instinct.

pos: n. (Lyman Beecher, 1775–1863, Connecticut and Ohio Presbyterian, revivalist, first president of Lane Theological Seminary)
etymology: English surname Beecher, a dweller by the beech trees; Lyman, from a place name, the meadow man.
biblical_def: Lyman Beecher trained under Timothy Dwight at Yale, pastored at East Hampton, Litchfield, and Boston, and in 1832 went west to be first president of Lane Theological Seminary in Cincinnati. He was the most energetic organiser of his generation: temperance societies, Sabbath observance, home missions, the campaign against duelling, and a vast programme for evangelising the Mississippi valley before Rome could settle it. He preached Taylor's doctrine of ability and was tried for heresy in 1835 by Joshua Lane Wilson of the Cincinnati presbytery on charges of denying original sin and teaching that regeneration is the sinner's own act; he was acquitted, appealed, and acquitted again, and the trial was one of the sparks of the Old School and New School division two years later. Eph 2:8 is the verse the charges turned on, that salvation is “the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heresy as a fundamental error in religion, and a presbytery as a body of elders in the Christian church.
webster_full: HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
PRES'BYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of all the pastors of churches within a certain district.
TRIAL, n. The examination of a cause in controversy between parties before a proper tribunal.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.
Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;
corruption_summary: The most effective organiser in American Protestantism, tried twice for the doctrine he preached.
corruption_paragraphs: Beecher is the point at which the New Haven theology became a movement rather than a lecture room. His energy carried Taylor's doctrine of native ability into the pulpits and societies of the West, and the revival technique followed it, because a doctrine of unimpaired power licenses any method that secures a decision. Eph 2:8 is the correction and it is brief: grace, through faith, “and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).

The dictionary does not treat Wilson's prosecution as mere ecclesiastical spite. Act 20:30 anticipates exactly this situation, men arising from within the body “speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30), and Rom 16:17 directs the church to mark the cause of division by its doctrine. That Beecher was acquitted twice is a judgment on the courts, not a vindication of the doctrine; the same assembly divided in 1837 over the questions his trial had raised. His organising instincts remain admirable and his theology of the will was the opening through which semi-Pelagianism entered American evangelicalism and stayed.
usage: “it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8) — the point of the charges against him.
“speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples” (Act 20:30) — the prosecution's text.
“mark them which cause divisions” (Rom 16:17) — marked by doctrine, not temper.

pos: n. (the practice and doctrine of Solomon Stoddard: admission of the unconverted but orderly to the Lord's Supper as a converting ordinance)
etymology: From the surname Stoddard + Greek -ismos, a system or practice.
biblical_def: Stoddardeanism is the name New England gave to the position Solomon Stoddard of Northampton argued from the 1670s onward: that the Lord's Supper is a converting ordinance, and that all adults of orderly life who profess the doctrines of religion may be admitted to it without a credible account of saving grace. Stoddard went further than the Half-Way Covenant, which had admitted the baptized but unconverted to baptism for their children while withholding the table; he opened the table itself. His reasoning was pastoral and sincere: the ordinance is a means of grace, and the unconverted most need means. Increase Mather opposed him in print for decades. His own grandson Jonathan Edwards reversed the practice at Northampton in 1749 and was dismissed from the pulpit for it. 1Co 11:28 is the verse the dispute turns on: “let a man examine himself” (1Co 11:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a communicant as one who partakes of the Lord's Supper, and an ordinance as an established rite or ceremony.
webster_full: COMMU'NICANT, n. One who partakes of the Lord's supper, or celebrates the eucharist.
ORD'INANCE, n. A rule established by authority; an institution; an established rite or ceremony.
ADMIS'SION, n. The act of admitting; allowance; the power or permission to enter.

corruption_summary: The table opened to the unconverted on the ground that they needed it most, and a grandson dismissed for closing it.
corruption_paragraphs: Stoddard's argument has a real pastoral motive and a decisive flaw. Paul does not treat the Supper as neutral toward the unworthy receiver: 1Co 11:29 says that he who eats and drinks unworthily “eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body” (1Co 11:29). An ordinance that harms the unprepared cannot be administered to the unprepared as a means of preparing them. The self-examination of 1Co 11:28 presupposes a communicant able to examine himself for faith, and the church's admission presupposes a credible profession.

The downstream effect in New England was a church membership increasingly indistinguishable from the town, which is the condition Edwards inherited and tried to reform. Mat 18:17 presumes a church with a boundary, since a man can only be put out of a body he was in. Act 2:42 describes the first communicants as those who continued in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship. The dictionary names Stoddardeanism as a corruption of the ordinance and notes the price Edwards paid for saying so: Northampton dismissed the greatest theologian in its history rather than restore the fence around the table.

pos: n. (John Wise, 1652–1725, pastor of Chebacco in Ipswich, Massachusetts, defender of congregational independency)
etymology: English surname Wise, from Old English wis, prudent, learned.
biblical_def: John Wise was pastor of the Chebacco parish in Ipswich for more than forty years. In 1687 he was jailed and fined for leading his town's refusal to pay a tax laid without an assembly by Governor Andros, and he argued at his trial that Englishmen could not be taxed without their own consent. Twenty years later he turned the same instinct on his own denomination. The Mather proposals of 1705 would have placed standing associations of ministers over the churches with power to examine candidates and settle disputes; Wise answered with The Churches Quarrel Espoused (1710) and A Vindication of the Government of New England Churches (1717), arguing that Christ gave authority to each particular congregation, that officers serve the body and do not rule over it, and that a ministerial association above the churches is a presbytery by another name. The proposals failed in Massachusetts. 1Pe 5:3 is his text, that elders are not “being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines independency as complete self-government, and a congregation as an assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
webster_full: INDEPEND'ENCY, n. Complete exemption from control, or the power of others; in church government, the system of Independents, who hold each church to be a complete body.
CONGREGA'TION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; an assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction.
VINDICA'TION, n. The act of vindicating; a justification against denial or censure; defense.
scriptures: Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
corruption_summary: He went to jail over a tax and then wrote the book that stopped the Mathers.
corruption_paragraphs: Wise's argument is the New England congregational case at its best. Mat 18:17 lodges the final earthly step of discipline in the congregation — “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — and an authority that can overrule the congregation on that point has taken the keys from the hands Christ put them in. 1Pe 5:3 forbids the lordship directly, and 1Pe 5:2 describes the office as feeding, not ruling for its own sake.

The dictionary holds local-church congregational governance with a plurality of elders, and so stands with Wise against the 1705 proposals, while declining his occasional drift toward arguing church order from natural liberty and the law of nations rather than from the New Testament. Act 15:6 shows apostles and elders taking counsel together, so consultation among churches is not forbidden; what is forbidden is a standing court above them. The distinction between a synod that advises and a presbytery that rules is the whole question, and Wise saw it clearly when his own side's most respected men did not.
